The first thing I stopped doing was the one I was best at, which I think is usually how it goes. I used to schedule the whole floor myself, every week, and I was quick at it because I had done it for eleven years. I handed it to a supervisor and the first month was worse. Not a disaster, but worse, and I had to sit on my hands and let it be worse, because if I had taken it back at that point I would have taken it back permanently. What I did instead was change what came to me. I still have the schedule sent to me on Friday, and I read it, and about once a month I ask a question about it. That is the whole of my involvement now. The thing nobody tells you is that the hard part is not handing over the work. The hard part is the six weeks after, when you can still do it faster than the person doing it.

I get called in when a company has grown and the person at the top is still working sixty hours, and almost every time the diagnosis is the same. It is not that they have not delegated. They have delegated a great deal. What they have not noticed is that the decisions keep coming back up, one at a time, disguised as questions. Somebody arrives at the door, asks whether they should do A or B, gets an answer, and everybody carries on believing the work is theirs. Nothing about that exchange looks like a failure. It takes ninety seconds and it feels helpful. But the deciding was the job, and it has just been handed back. What I ask a director to do for two weeks is not to stop answering, because that is unfair, but to answer with a question. What would you do. Nine times out of ten they already know, and about the tenth time you have found a genuine escalation, which is exactly the one you wanted to see.
